Here are the verse-by-verse notes, compiled from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Mark 4:1-20 – The Parable of the Sower (Soils)

### v. 1 — Jesus teaches beside the sea from a boat

Jesus returned to teach by the lakeshore because the crowds had become so large that indoor spaces (the house at Capernaum) could no longer hold them. Mark uses the Greek superlative *πλεῖστος* (“a very great” multitude), the largest crowd yet recorded. Jesus entered a boat and sat — the typical posture of a rabbi teaching — so that His voice would carry across the water (natural acoustics) and He would not be crushed by the press. This was a practical “pulpit.” Mark notes this was the same day as the earlier events in chapter 3 (the accusation about Beelzebub and the visit of Jesus’ mother and brothers).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “Jesus often used a boat as His ‘pulpit’ … it provided good acoustics, and it was probably a nice backdrop.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “he went out of the house where he was at Capernaum, the same day … to the sea side, the shore of the sea of Galilee.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek πλεῖστος indicates “a very great multitude.”

### v. 2 — Jesus teaches in parables

This marks a decisive shift in Jesus’ method. Before this, He taught plainly; now He uses parables. Mark 4 contains four parables and is the longest teaching block in Mark. The Greek *παραβολή* (parabolē) means “to cast alongside” — a spiritual truth set beside an everyday reality. But as Jesus used them at this stage, parables were not simple illustrations; they were riddles or doorways — revealing truth to those with receptive hearts and concealing it from those hardened against Him.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-4-commentary — “Beginning here in Mark 4 we see a shift … parables are given not to reveal but to hide truths from those who not have hearts to hear.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “The word parable comes from the idea of ‘to set along side.’”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit: “This was a new system of teaching … he abandoned [direct teaching] for the less direct method of the parable.”

### v. 3 — “Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed”

The word “Listen!” (Ἀκούετε) is unique to Mark’s account and sets up the warning in v. 9 (“He who has ears to hear, let him hear”). Commentators identify the Sower primarily as Christ Himself — the great Preacher of the gospel — and by extension every faithful minister of the Word. Gill says the sower is Christ “who came forth from God as a teacher, and went out into the land of Judea to preach the Gospel.” In the Eastern agricultural setting, fields were open and unfenced, with footpaths running through them, so seed falling in varied places was normal, not careless farming.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit: “Christ teaches us that he is the Sower, that is, the great Preacher of the gospel among men.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “By whom is meant Jesus Christ … and this may be also applicable to any faithful minister of the word.”
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower — Spurgeon describes the Eastern open-field practice: “through these open lands there are footpaths … he must throw a handful upon it.”

### v. 4 — Seed on the path; birds devour it

The “wayside” (path) was ground beaten hard by constant foot-traffic — unploughed, impenetrable. The seed could not enter the soil and lay exposed. The birds represent Satan and his agents who snatch the word away. Luke adds the detail that the seed was “trodden down” before being eaten. The heart represented here is one calloused by habitual sin, crowded with worldly traffic — the word never enters.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/4-4.htm — JFB: “by the side of the hard path through the field, where the soil was not broken up … Not only could the seed not get beneath the surface, but ‘it was trodden down’ (Luke 8:5).”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “the common beaten path: the word was dispensed among some men comparable to it, on whom it lighted, but made no impression.”
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower — Spurgeon: “Your heart is just like those crowded thoroughfares; for so many cares and sins throng it … that the seed of truth cannot grow.”

### vv. 5-6 — Seed on rocky ground; springs up quickly, then withers

This is not soil full of stones but a thin layer of topsoil over a limestone bedrock — common in Galilee. The seed germinates rapidly because the shallow soil warms quickly, producing a flash of growth. But with no depth for roots to reach moisture, the plant is scorched when the sun rises. The scorching sun represents tribulation or persecution (see v. 17). The hearer represented receives the word with immediate joy, makes a hasty profession, but has “no root in themselves” — no genuine inward work of grace, only emotional excitement.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “the word was preached to some persons who had hearts of stone … a sudden and hasty profession of the word was made, without a powerful experience of it.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — quoting Spurgeon: “Then there are many more, whose religion must be sustained by enthusiastic surroundings … the religion that is born of mere excitement will die when the excitement is over.”
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower — Spurgeon: “They have no deep convictions, but they leap into Christ on a sudden … We enquire when the good work began. We find it began when it ended.”

### v. 7 — Seed among thorns; choked, yields no crop

This soil is actually fertile — thorns grow well there, indicating good soil. The problem is competition. The thorns (worldly cares, deceitfulness of riches, desires for other things — see v. 19) grow alongside the wheat and eventually choke it. The Greek word in Mark is συνέπνιξαν, “choked together.” The plant may reach the ear stage but produces no mature grain. The hearer represented makes a genuine start but allows competing loyalties to suffocate spiritual life. Unlike the rocky-ground hearer who falls away through persecution, this hearer falls through prosperity and distraction.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit: “not all who show faith bring forth the fruit of good works … the thorns grew up with it and choked it.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “the word did not take place so as to beat down, overcome, and root out these things … these got the ascendant of the word.”
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower — Spurgeon: “This was good soil … Wherever a thistle will spring up and flourish, there would wheat flourish too. This was fat, fertile soil … See how happy he is when in a month or two he visits the spot. The seed has sprung up … [but later] the thorns, and the briars have become intertwisted … it never comes to anything.”

### v. 8 — Seed on good soil; thirty, sixty, hundredfold

The good ground represents the heart prepared by God to receive the word. All four soils hear the same seed; the difference is the soil. Mark’s account gives an ascending scale (thirty → sixty → hundred), whereas Matthew gives a descending scale — a minor variation sufficient to show Mark’s independence as an author (noted by Ellicott). Not all good soil produces identically; there are gradations of fruitfulness. This may reflect differing measures of grace, differing diligence in co-operating with grace, or differing God-given capacities and opportunities.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/4.htm — Ellicott notes “an ascending instead of a descending scale … sufficient to establish a certain measure of independence.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit: “this on account of the greater influences of grace, or on account of the more ready co-operation of the free-will of man with the sovereign grace of God.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “Of the seed that fell on the good ground, all of it produced – but not all produced to the same degree.”

### v. 9 — “He who has ears to hear, let him hear”

This call — literally “let him be hearing” — is Jesus’ invitation to press beyond the surface story. It is a test: the spiritually hungry will seek the meaning; the indifferent will walk away with just an agricultural anecdote. The phrase appears multiple times in the Gospels and Revelation as a summons to spiritual attentiveness.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — (Paraphrasing G. Campbell Morgan) “Jesus used the parabolic method … in order to lure them toward a new attention.”
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-4-commentary — “only those men and women who have ‘ears to hear’ will be able to understand the deeper meaning.”

### v. 10 — The disciples ask about the parable

“Those around Him with the Twelve” indicates a wider circle than just the apostles — perhaps the seventy or other committed followers. They waited until Jesus was alone (away from the crowd) to ask. The fact that even the disciples did not understand this parable shows that parables are not self-interpreting; they require the key that only Jesus supplies.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “Notice that even with this ‘simple’ parable, the disciples themselves do not understand.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “they that were about him with the twelve … such disciples of his, who, besides the twelve, constantly attended him; perhaps … the seventy disciples.”

### v. 11 — The mystery of the kingdom given to you; to outsiders, parables

“Mystery” (μυστήριον) in the biblical sense is not something puzzling but something previously hidden that God must reveal — you would not know it unless God disclosed it. The disciples are “insiders” who receive direct revelation. “Those outside” is a phrase unique to Mark (Matthew has “to them”; Luke has “to the rest”) — it designates not just the hostile but all who lack the disciples’ responsive faith. To them, “everything is expressed in parables” — i.e., their entire encounter with Jesus’ teaching is now veiled.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/4.htm — Ellicott: “The form of the phrase is peculiar to St. Mark … ‘Unto them that are without.’”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “In the Bible, a mystery isn’t something you can’t figure out. It is something that you would not know unless God revealed it to you.”
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-4-commentary — “From now on, only those men and women who have ‘ears to hear’ will be able to understand … Some would consider this change … a form of ‘judicial hardening.’”

### v. 12 — The Isaiah 6:9-10 quotation

Jesus quotes Isaiah’s commission, where the prophet is told his preaching will actually harden those who resist. Mark does not present it as a formal quotation (no introductory formula), and the wording is less precise than Matthew’s. The saying is startling: it *sounds* as if Jesus teaches in parables *in order to* prevent repentance and forgiveness. But commentators across traditions explain this as a Semitic way of expressing a *result* as if it were a *purpose*. Jesus did not intend to blind people; rather, His parabolic method was an act of judgment on already hardened hearts — and simultaneously an act of mercy, because it reduced their culpability (less light, less condemnation). Those who had already rejected plain teaching would not be given more light to reject.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/4.htm — Ellicott: “The real meaning of the words is … This was to be the result of the wilful blindness of those who rejected Him; and the acceptance of a foreseen result was, in Hebrew forms of thought, expressed as the working out of an intention.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “Jesus didn’t use parables to blind people, but because they were blind … ‘in order to lure them toward a new attention.’” (quoting Morgan)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — quoting Geldenhuys: “so that their guilt may not accumulate, the Lord no longer addresses them directly in explicit teachings … but in parables.”

### v. 13 — “Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any?”

Jesus’ question (unique to Mark) is gently rebuking. This parable is foundational; it is the “key” to all parabolic teaching. If the disciples cannot grasp this one — where Jesus Himself provides the interpretation — how will they understand others? The question also implies that understanding the parables is not optional but essential, and that there is an expected trajectory of growing insight for disciples. Gill notes the parable is drawn from common life and should be “easy to be understood.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “Jesus considered this parable as essential to understanding His other parables.”
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/4.htm — Ellicott: “The question is peculiar to St. Mark, and suggests the thought of our Lord as contemplating for His disciples an ever-growing insight … The first lesson in interpreting is given in that which is a pattern and exemplar of the method of interpretation.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “So easy to be understood, taken from things common, and which fall under every one’s observation.”

### v. 14 — “The farmer sows the word”

This is the interpretive key to the whole parable. The seed is “the word” — Mark uses the absolute term, while Matthew calls it “the word of the kingdom” (Mt 13:19) and Luke “the word of God” (Lk 8:11). If you miss this, you miss everything: the seed is not money, love, hard work, or good deeds — it is God’s revealed truth. The Sower is not explicitly identified here, but from the parable and context it is Christ (and derivatively all who preach His word). The Pulpit Commentary calls it “the gospel of the kingdom, not merely moral truth, but spiritual and eternal.”

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “If you miss the key, you miss the whole parable … You can only understand it by understanding the key: The sower sows the word.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit: “St. Matthew (Matthew 13:19) calls it ‘the word of the kingdom’ — an expression equivalent to ‘the gospel of the kingdom,’ not merely moral truth, but spiritual and eternal.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “the seed … is the word of God … the word of life and truth; the word of peace and reconciliation; the word of faith and righteousness; the word of salvation.”

### v. 15 — The path hearers: Satan snatches the word

The wayside hearers are those whose hearts are hardened — calloused by constant traffic of worldly concerns. The word lies on the surface and never penetrates. “Satan” (Mark) is “the evil one” (Matthew) — the same figure named in the Lord’s Prayer (“deliver us from the evil one”). Mark emphasizes the immediacy: “immediately” (εὐθὺς, Mark’s characteristic word) Satan comes. He does not want the word to take root. The Pulpit Commentary draws the connection that just as the hardened path makes the seed easy prey for birds, so a heart “rendered callous by the custom of sinning” makes the word easy prey for the devil.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit: “As the seed failing by the wayside is refused by the hard and well-trodden ground … in like manner, the seed of God’s Word, falling upon a heart rendered callous by the custom of sinning, is straightway snatched away by ‘the evil one.’”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “Satan doesn’t want the word of God to take root in a person’s heart … This is Satan’s preferred result.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “whilst they are hearing … Satan cometh immediately … filling their minds with other things suitable to their dispositions.”

### vv. 16-17 — The rocky-ground hearers: joy, no root, fall away

These hearers “immediately receive it with joy.” The problem is not lack of emotion but lack of depth. Their root is not in Christ but in circumstances — “no root in themselves.” They endure “for a season” (πρόσκαιροι, temporary). When “tribulation or persecution arises because of the word,” they “immediately stumble” (σκανδαλίζονται — are scandalised, caused to trip). The stony-ground hearer is not attacked by Satan directly (as in v. 15) but by hardship that tests the genuineness of faith. Enduring Word quotes Spurgeon: many have their root in parents, Christian friends, a pastor, or enthusiastic surroundings — not in Christ.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “The stony ground hearer isn’t attacked directly by Satan, but by tribulation or persecution.”
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower — Spurgeon: “They have no root in themselves … Their religion must be sustained by enthusiastic surroundings … the religion that is born of mere excitement will die when the excitement is over.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “the word has no root in their hearts, only in their natural affections: nor is the root of grace in them; there is no heart work, only speculative notions, and flashy affections.”

### vv. 18-19 — The thorny-ground hearers: choked by cares, riches, pleasures

Three specific “thorns” are named: (1) “the cares of this world” — anxious distractions; (2) “the deceitfulness of riches” — wealth that promises satisfaction but lies; (3) “the desires for other things” — the broad category of all other lusts and ambitions that compete with the word. These “enter in” and “choke” (συμπνίγουσιν, choke together) the word. The result is not apostasy but unfruitfulness — the plant exists but yields no harvest. Gill notes that these hearers are “of worldly dispositions … immoderately careful and anxious about the things of this life.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “the cares of this world … the deceitfulness of riches … the lusts of other things entering in … choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “We might say this ground is too fertile. The word of God grows there, but so does everything else.”
- https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower — Spurgeon’s extended treatment notes that this soil is good soil (thorns grow well), and the tragedy is that the hearer comes close to fruitfulness but never reaches maturity: “It never comes to anything. With it the reaper never fills his arm.”

### v. 20 — The good-ground hearers: hear, accept, bear fruit

The good soil represents those who (1) hear the word, (2) “accept” or “receive” it (παραδέχονται — welcome it), and (3) bear fruit. The fruit is the proof of genuine reception. The threefold harvest (thirty, sixty, hundred) shows that among true believers there is variety in fruitfulness — not all produce equally. Reasons suggested include: differing measures of grace, differing levels of diligence in cooperating with grace, differing natural capacities and callings, and differing degrees of applying the Word. St. Jerome (cited by Pulpit) observed that just as there are three kinds of bad soil, there is a threefold gradation of good soil.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html — Pulpit: “The good ground represents the heart which receives the Word of God with joy and desire, and true devotion of spirit, and which steadfastly retains it … St. Jerome remarks that … of the good ground there is a threefold gradation.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html — Gill: “all bring forth good fruit of the same quality, though not of the same quantity.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/ — “This parable shows that when the word is received as it should be, something happens – fruit is produced. If nothing happens, then the word is not being received as it should.”

---

## Denominational Distinctives

**Baptist (Reformed Baptist / Particular Baptist):**
Spurgeon and Gill both stress that the seed is God’s sovereign gift (the preacher “does not make his seed; it is given him by his divine Master”) and that the soils represent God’s sovereign work in hearts. Yet Spurgeon also stresses human responsibility in hearing — the hearer is accountable for what kind of soil he is. Gill treats the good soil as “those who are made good men by the grace of God; for there is none good naturally.” (Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-parable-of-the-sower ; Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/mark-4.html)

**Reformed / Presbyterian:**
Through the Ligonier and Enduring Word connections (David Guzik draws on Reformed sources), the emphasis is that the parable critiques the hearer, not the preacher: “The natural tendency is for the audience to critique the preacher. But here, Jesus the preacher critiques His audience.” The sovereignty of God is seen in the “mystery” given to the disciples (v. 11) versus its concealment from outsiders. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):**
The commentary emphasises spiritual warfare — Satan actively and immediately snatches the word (v. 15) — and the power of the Word itself as a living seed with inherent vitality. The “mystery” of kingdom growth is that the Word works invisibly and powerfully, like a seed germinating in the dark. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-4/)

**Methodist / Wesleyan / Arminian:**
The Pulpit Commentary, while broadly Anglican/evangelical, contains the distinctively Arminian note that differing fruitfulness is “on account of the greater influences of grace, or on account of the more ready co-operation of the free-will of man with the sovereign grace of God.” This explicit pairing of grace and human free-will cooperation is characteristic of Wesleyan-Arminian theology. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/mark-4.html)

**Evangelical (Precept Austin):**
Precept Austin (non-denominational conservative evangelical) stresses that the parable marks a “judicial hardening” — not because Jesus desired to harden, but because persistent rejection of plain teaching resulted in parabolic veiling. It also emphasises that understanding parables requires the indwelling Spirit: “If you are truly born again, then the Father and the Son have given you the gift of the Spirit of Truth Who now lives in you to enable you to understand spiritual truth.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-4-commentary)
